newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Hungary, Czechs lead central Europe FDI surge - UN.
newsitem.headline: Hungary, Czechs lead central Europe FDI surge - UN.

text.p: Foreign direct investment (FDI) in the five countries of the Central European Free Trade Area (CEFTA) more than doubled in 1995 to $8.890 billion, the United Nations said on Wednesday.

The World Investment Report by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said Hungary and the Czech Republic led CEFTA in their rate of FDI growth, while Poland, Slovakia, and Slovenia posted relatively solid gains.
Mainly due to privatisations, inflows into Hungary and the Czech Republic tripled to $3.5 billion and $2.5 billion respectively.
The European Union comprises most of the direct investment in the region holding three quarters of FDI stock in Hungary and two thirds in the Czech Republic, Poland, Slovakia, and Slovenia, it said.

"(The EU) is the most important trading partner for all (central/eastern European) countries, reflecting intra-firm trade flows...and the importance of the region as a production base for exports to the European Union," it said.

Some 60 percent of the Czech Republic's inflows in 1995 were related to the privatisation of its telecommunications monopoly SPT Telecom a.s. and oil refineries, and Hungary's rise also was due largely to its telecommunications sell-off.
"Inflows into the Czech Republic and Hungary are, however, much more volatile because much is related to privatisation," the report said.

Non-privatisation-related FDI inflows in the so-called Visegrad countries were higher in Poland than in Hungary and the Czech Republic, UNCTAD said, "reflecting the better growth performance of the former."
"Among the Visegrad countries, Poland was the first to make the turnaround in economic growth after the initial transition shock," it said.
The report showed small but steady FDI growth in CEFTA aspirants, with 1995 inflows increasing to $135 million from $106 million in Bulgaria and to $373 million from $340 million in 1994 in Romania.
